title: NASA-IBM's Surya AI Model Predicts Solar Flares Hours Before They Strike
excerpt: The open-source foundation model, trained on a decade of NASA satellite imagery, marks a leap in forecasting violent solar eruptions that threaten satellites, power grids, and communications systems worldwide.
body:
• NASA and IBM's Surya AI model can predict solar flares up to two hours in advance with 16% better accuracy than previous methods
  • Trained on 250 terabytes of data from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory spanning nine years of high-resolution solar imagery
  • A separate NYU Abu Dhabi study by Indian-origin researchers achieved four-day solar wind forecasts with 45% improvement over existing models
  • Surya is open source and available on Hugging Face, enabling researchers worldwide to build specialized space weather applications

NASA and IBM have released Surya, the first foundation model for solar physics, trained on nine years of high-resolution imagery from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory to forecast solar flares, wind speeds, and active regions on the sun's surface.

The model — named after the Sanskrit word for "sun" — represents a shift from narrowly focused prediction tools to a versatile AI system capable of identifying hidden patterns in solar data that human analysts might miss. In early testing, Surya predicted the strength of solar flares 16% more accurately than previous methods and, for the first time, enabled researchers to visually forecast where on the sun's surface a flare would occur up to two hours in advance.

"By developing a foundation model trained on NASA's heliophysics data, we're making it easier to analyze the complexities of the sun's behavior with unprecedented speed and precision."

— Kevin Murphy, Chief Science Data Officer, NASA Headquarters

Why Solar Storm Prediction Matters

The stakes are enormous. Solar flares and coronal mass ejections can knock out satellites, disrupt airline navigation, trigger power blackouts, and pose radiation risks to astronauts. A Lloyd's systemic risk analysis estimates that a severe solar storm could expose the global economy to $2.4 trillion in losses over a five-year period.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=x82IwfbZMzo

The sun is currently near the peak of its 11-year activity cycle, making accurate forecasting more urgent than ever. In 2022, a strong solar wind event caused SpaceX to lose 40 Starlink satellites shortly after launch — a stark demonstration of the damage space weather can inflict on modern infrastructure.

"Think of this as a weather forecast for space," said Juan Bernabé-Moreno, director of IBM Research Europe for the U.K. and Ireland. "Just as we work to prepare for hazardous weather events, we need to do the same for solar storms. Surya gives us unprecedented capability to anticipate what's coming."

How Surya Works

The model was trained on more than 250 terabytes of data from the Solar Dynamics Observatory, which orbits Earth at an altitude of 22,200 miles and captures images of the sun in 13 different wavelengths every 12 seconds. These solar images are roughly 10 times larger than typical AI training data, requiring IBM to develop a custom multi-architecture system to handle the scale.

Researchers fed Surya sequential images and challenged it to predict what the SDO would observe an hour into the future, then checked those predictions against actual observations. The model learned the sun's physical quirks — including its differential rotation, where the equator spins faster than the poles — more effectively from the raw data than from any human-coded parameters.

"It's just those tiny destabilizations that we know happen, but we don't know when," said Louise Harra, an astrophysicist at ETH Zurich who was not involved in the project. "The promise of Surya lies in whether it can find the patterns underlying those destabilizations faster than any existing methods, buying us extra time."

Complementary Research Extends Forecast Window

While Surya focuses on short-term prediction, a separate study by researchers at NYU Abu Dhabi has pushed the forecast window further out. A team led by Dattaraj Dhuri and Shravan Hanasoge developed an AI model that can predict solar wind speeds up to four days in advance — a 45% improvement over current operational models and 20% better than previous AI-based approaches. The study was published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series.

"By combining advanced AI with solar observations, we can give early warnings that help safeguard critical technology on Earth and in space."

— Dattaraj Dhuri, Lead Author, NYU Abu Dhabi

India's Growing Role in Solar Science

India's Aditya-L1 mission, which reached the Sun-Earth L1 Lagrange point in January 2024, is generating its own trove of solar data from dedicated soft and hard X-ray instruments. ISRO's first solar observatory has already spawned multiple AI-based prediction projects through initiatives like the Bharatiya Antariksh Hackathon, with teams building flare forecasting tools using Aditya-L1 telemetry data.

The Surya model itself draws on a global tradition of solar observation. Its open-source release on Hugging Face, GitHub, and IBM's TerraTorch library means researchers in India and beyond can fine-tune the model for regional applications and integrate it with data from missions like Aditya-L1.

What Comes Next

Bernabé-Moreno sees applications beyond flare prediction. He hopes to combine Surya with earlier NASA-IBM weather models — part of the Prithvi family of foundation models for Earth science — to study how solar storms influence terrestrial weather, including potential links to lightning activity.

"Understanding the sun is a proxy for understanding many other stars," Bernabé-Moreno said. "We look at the sun as a laboratory."
